item.title: AI-assisted intrusions are here: what the ARTEX warning changes for defenders
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The FBI warns an AI pentesting framework is powering real intrusions, and the European Commission confirms an AI-assisted attack. A CTO's take on what to change now.
item.content:encoded:
In one week, the FBI warned that an autonomous AI penetration testing framework is being used in real intrusions, some reaching privileged access in under three hours, and the European Commission confirmed that an AI-assisted attack disrupted its staff systems. The techniques are not new. The speed, persistence and cost are. That changes which defences matter most.

What was reported

On 13 November the FBI issued a FLASH warning about ARTEX, an autonomous penetration testing framework that uses AI agents connected to external language models to plan and chain attack techniques1. The FBI says it is being used in real intrusions, and that some went from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours2. Reporting says the tool was published openly, later withdrawn, and remains available through forks and a commercial edition, and that attackers favour cheap models that do not refuse requests framed as penetration testing5. Targets span sectors including energy, manufacturing and telecoms3.

Days later, the European Commission confirmed that an AI-assisted cyberattack detected in October disrupted staff systems including HR, medical reimbursement and translation services, some for more than ten days4. Press reports link that campaign to the same framework; the Commission has not confirmed it.

What actually changes

Nothing in the reporting describes a new class of vulnerability. An AI agent running a penetration testing framework uses the same techniques a human tester would. Three things change, and each shifts which defences matter.

The cost point matters most for mid-sized companies. Attacks that used to need skilled people were reserved for valuable targets. When an agent can do the reconnaissance and chaining for the price of model calls, the threshold drops, and organisations that relied on not being interesting lose that protection.

Defences that work at machine speed

If an attacker can chain techniques in hours, a defence that depends on a person noticing an alert the next morning is too slow. The controls that hold up are the ones that sit in the path of every request and decide automatically. Kubernetes admission control is a good model: every API request passes authentication, authorisation, then mutating and validating checks before anything changes6. The same idea applies across an estate: put the decision where the action happens.

ControlWhy it matters more now
Shrink what is exposedAn agent will find every internet-facing service; fewer services means fewer chances
Phishing-resistant sign-in for staff and adminsCredential theft remains the cheapest first step to automate
Patch exposed systems in daysExploits for published flaws are chained faster than monthly cycles allow
Segment management planesA foothold should not reach identity, virtualisation or backups directly
Automated containmentDisable accounts and isolate hosts on high-confidence signals without waiting for a person
Short-lived credentialsStolen tokens should expire before an agent finishes using them

The test: if an attacker got a foothold at 2am on a Saturday, what stops them reaching an administrator account before Monday? If the answer is a person reading alerts, that is the gap.

Use the same tools on yourself

The uncomfortable corollary is that defenders can use these frameworks too. Running an autonomous testing tool against your own external surface, with permission and in a controlled scope, shows what an attacker's agent would find, faster than an annual penetration test. The governance matters: a defined scope, approved models, logging of every action and a kill switch. The same controls I describe for production agents in prompt injection defences and agent sandboxing apply to security agents.

The CTO's take

AI-assisted attacks are less a new threat than a price cut on old ones. The organisations most affected will be the ones that relied on being too small or too obscure to bother with, and the ones whose response depends on business hours. The fixes are familiar and unglamorous: expose less, authenticate strongly, patch the edge quickly and let systems contain obvious compromise automatically. This month's incidents, from vendor admin tools to the vCenter campaign, show where to start. For regulated firms, the AI cyber risk controls case study shows how this maps to supervisory expectations.

If you want a quick, honest view of how your estate would hold up against an automated attacker, I am a fractional CTO and AI architect based in India, the United States and the UAE, working globally. You can analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: Tech news, 21 November 2026: the European Commission's AI-assisted attack, how the vCenter campaign began, a TfL breach and Anthropic's Texas data centre
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: the European Commission confirms an AI-assisted cyberattack, vCenter attacks are traced to a BeyondTrust zero-day, TfL is breached, Anthropic's Texas lease.
item.content:encoded:
The European Commission confirmed that an AI-assisted cyberattack disrupted staff services for days. Google's researchers traced the vCenter zero-day campaign to a China-linked group that first broke in through a BeyondTrust remote support flaw. Transport for London disclosed a breach of Oyster photocard accounts, and a filing named Anthropic as the tenant of a large Texas data centre lease.

Today's brief covers stories from 19 to 20 November.

1. The European Commission confirms an AI-assisted cyberattack

The European Commission confirmed that an AI-assisted cyberattack, detected on 22 October, disrupted staff services including its HR platform Sysper, the MyPMO medical reimbursement system and translation services, with some outages lasting more than ten days1. The Commission says it has found no evidence of a data breach so far and that the investigation continues; press reports link the campaign to a publicly available AI penetration testing framework, which the Commission has not confirmed2.

CTO take: the practical change from AI-assisted attacks is speed and persistence, not new techniques. Attackers can try more paths, faster, against everything you expose. That makes the basics more urgent: phishing-resistant sign-in, quick patching of internet-facing systems, segmentation so one compromised service does not reach the rest, and detection tuned to spot rapid, automated reconnaissance. European public bodies and their suppliers should expect questions on exactly these controls. See the AI cyber risk controls case study and my Europe page.

2. The vCenter zero-day campaign began with a BeyondTrust flaw

Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group attribute exploitation of the vCenter authentication bypass to Armory Castle, a suspected China-nexus espionage group, which first compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support instances through a separate zero-day in late August, then moved to an internal appliance and on to vCenter from early September3. Google says a small number of organisations are confirmed compromised and others are likely affected4.

CTO take: this is the pattern from this month's vendor admin access analysis playing out: a remote access tool at the edge, then the virtualisation control plane. If you run BeyondTrust Remote Support or vCenter, patch both, then hunt rather than assume: look for new administrator and single sign-on accounts, unusual vCenter logins and unexpected outbound traffic from management appliances since late August. Keep management interfaces on networks that remote support tools cannot reach directly.

3. Transport for London discloses an Oyster photocard breach

Transport for London said about 265,000 Oyster photocard customers were affected after it detected suspicious activity on 16 November and took the photocard system offline; reported exposed data includes names, contact details, addresses and security questions and answers5. TfL says passwords and payment card details were not compromised, and customers will be asked to reset passwords and security answers when the portal returns6.

CTO take: security questions are the weak point here. Once their answers leak, they are useful to attackers on every other service that uses the same questions, and customers cannot change their mother's maiden name. If your product still uses knowledge-based questions for recovery, replace them with stronger recovery factors. UK organisations should also note how quickly the regulator was informed. See the access hardening case study and my UK page.

4. A filing names Anthropic as tenant of a $28 billion Texas lease

Riot Platforms had disclosed a 15-year lease of its Corsicana, Texas campus to a frontier AI lab, with total contract value of about $28 billion7. Its latest quarterly filing names Anthropic as the tenant8.

CTO take: long leases like this are how AI providers secure future capacity, and they are a useful signal for customers. A provider that has locked in power and space is better placed to honour capacity commitments, but also carries fixed costs that shape its pricing. When negotiating, ask providers about capacity guarantees and regions, not just per-token prices. See AI capacity contracts and the multi-region AI capacity case study.

What I'd do this week

  • Patch BeyondTrust Remote Support and vCenter, then hunt for new admin and SSO accounts since late August.
  • Check that management interfaces are unreachable from remote support and user networks.
  • Replace security questions in account recovery with stronger factors.
  • Review detection for fast, automated reconnaissance against internet-facing services.
  • Ask AI providers about capacity guarantees in your regions at the next renewal.

I am a fractional CTO and AI architect based in India, the United States and the UAE, working globally. If any of these lands on your desk this week, analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: Tech news, 20 November 2026: a critical vCenter bypass, Malaysia and US chip rules, UK AI cyber practices and Anthropic's market debut
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: a critical vCenter authentication bypass, Malaysia tells data centres to follow US chip rules, UK regulators set AI cyber practices, Anthropic lists.
item.content:encoded:
Broadcom patched a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter, with reports that it was exploited before the fix. Malaysia told its data centre operators to comply with the new US rules on advanced chips as Washington offered support for a Malaysian sovereign AI cloud. UK financial regulators published effective practices for AI-related cyber risk, and Anthropic's shares began trading on Nasdaq.

Today's brief covers stories from 18 to 19 November.

1. Broadcom patches a critical vCenter authentication bypass

Broadcom's advisory VMSA-2026-0009 fixes five flaws across vCenter, SDDC Manager and VMware Tools, the most serious being CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter gain access; there is no workaround1. BleepingComputer reports the flaw was exploited as a zero-day since September by China-linked attackers2; Broadcom's advisory itself is reported not to describe exploitation, so treat that as reported rather than confirmed by the vendor.

CTO take: vCenter is the control plane for every virtual machine it manages, so this is a patch-tonight item for anyone running it. Patch, then check: review vCenter authentication and administrative activity since September, and confirm vCenter is reachable only from a management network, never from user networks or the internet. If you are still on a version without a public fix, that is the moment to fund the upgrade. See admin tools as perimeter and the management plane hardening case study.

2. Malaysia tells data centres to follow US chip rules, as the US backs its sovereign AI cloud

The US rule on remote access to advanced semiconductors was published in the Federal Register on 19 November3. Malaysia's trade minister said data centre operators must comply, including licences for advanced chips, and that the government would notify approved data centre projects and seek clarification from the US on licensing and third-party services4. Separately, Bloomberg reports the US will offer $50 million to support Malaysia's sovereign AI cloud5.

CTO take: for anyone buying GPU capacity in Malaysia, the practical effect is more know-your-customer questions from providers and some uncertainty about how third-party cloud services will be licensed. Keep your ownership and end-use information ready, avoid single-provider dependence in the region while the detail settles, and check contract terms for what happens if a provider loses a licence. See the Malaysia GPU cloud case study and my Southeast Asia page.

3. UK financial regulators publish AI cyber risk practices

The Bank of England, PRA and FCA published a consultation on cyber risk and resilience management, CP17/26 and GC26/9, which clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements and is open until 26 February 20277. Alongside it, a separate effective practices paper sets out how firms and financial market infrastructures are managing cyber risk related to AI, including reducing their attack surface against AI-enabled attacks6.

CTO take: effective practices are not rules, but they become the benchmark supervisors use in conversations. UK banks, insurers and payment firms should map their AI use, including agents and third-party models, against the practices now, and respond to the consultation if the expectations do not fit how they actually operate. Firms outside the UK can use it as a free, well-reasoned checklist. See the UK cyber resilience case study and my UK page.

4. Anthropic's shares begin trading

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, raising more than $81 billion in the largest offering on record8. Its shares opened on Nasdaq on 19 November at $111.50, TechRepublic reports9, and later closed lower than that opening price.

CTO take: for customers, a listed AI supplier means more public disclosure about capacity, costs and risks, which is useful in vendor reviews, and more pressure on revenue, which can show up in pricing and packaging. Neither changes the basic advice: keep a model gateway so you can switch providers, and track each provider's terms as carefully as their benchmarks. See LLM model routing and the AI provider resilience case study.

What I'd do this week

  • Patch vCenter, restrict access to a management network and review activity since September.
  • If you use GPU capacity in Malaysia, ask providers how the US licensing affects your service and contract.
  • UK financial firms: compare AI and agent use against the new effective practices and plan a consultation response.
  • Check that you could move your main AI workloads to a second provider without a rewrite.

I am a fractional CTO and AI architect based in India, the United States and the UAE, working globally. If any of these lands on your desk this week, analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: The agent-framework hack: why installing a package was enough to lose your cloud secrets
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Poisoned agent-framework releases stole cloud and CI secrets at Python start-up. A CTO's take on .pth hooks, why agent tooling is a prime target and what to change in CI.
item.content:encoded:
Two releases of Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI carried a credential stealer that ran every time Python started, whether or not anyone imported the package. The mechanism is an old, documented Python feature. The target was the place where agent tooling now lives: developer laptops and CI runners full of cloud credentials. Here is what happened, why it worked, and what to change.

What happened

On 17 November, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of agent-framework, Microsoft's Python package for building AI agents, were published to PyPI with a credential stealer targeting Azure, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions secrets1. Both have been removed, and Microsoft has said it is investigating2. Wiz identifies 1.26.0 as the latest safe version3.

Two details matter more than the headline. The releases appeared under the legitimate publisher rather than a lookalike name, and JFrog reports the attacker repacked the clean release rather than compromising Microsoft's build, which points to stolen publishing credentials4. And the two malicious versions went out within about half an hour of each other, the second moving the payload to a new file5. Anyone whose tooling upgraded automatically in that window got it.

Why installing was enough

The payload was delivered through a .pth file. Python's site module processes these path configuration files at start-up, and executes any line that begins with import6. It is a documented feature meant for setting up paths. It also means any installed package can run code every time Python starts, in every script, test run and notebook in that environment, without ever being imported4.

That changes the usual reasoning about risk. Teams often assume a dependency is only dangerous on the code paths that call it. Start-up hooks, install scripts and build plugins break that assumption: the risk is in the environment, not the call graph.

Why agent tooling is the target

Agent frameworks are installed where the valuable credentials are. Developers run them on laptops signed in to cloud consoles; CI pipelines run their tests with deployment credentials loaded; agents themselves are often given broad tokens so they can call tools. A package that sits in those environments is worth more to an attacker than almost any library in production, where secrets are usually narrower and better managed.

They are also young, fast-moving and upgraded eagerly. Teams building with agents want the newest release, so loose version ranges and automatic updates are common. That is exactly the window this attack used.

What to change in CI and developer environments

The CNCF's software supply chain paper treats build infrastructure as needing the same security as the production it builds for, and recommends single-use build workers so a compromise cannot persist or spread across builds7. Most of the fixes here follow from taking that seriously.

ControlWhat it stopsCost
Lockfiles with hashes for every installSilently picking up a new releaseLow; needs a routine for updates
A cooling-off period before new releases are allowedInstalling a release in its first hours, when most poisoned versions are caughtLow; small delay on fixes
Separate install and secret-holding steps in CIStart-up hooks reading deployment credentials during testsMedium; pipeline changes
Short-lived, narrowly scoped CI credentialsStolen secrets being useful for long or broadlyMedium; identity federation work
Single-use build workersA compromise persisting across buildsMedium; often already available
Internal package mirror with policyUnreviewed packages reaching any environmentHigher; worth it at scale

The most effective single change is keeping deployment credentials out of any step that installs or runs third-party code. Tests do not need the keys to production.

For developers, the equivalent is not running agent experiments in the same environment, or with the same signed-in cloud session, as production administration. A disposable container or virtual environment with no standing credentials costs little and limits what a poisoned package can find.

If you installed an affected version

  • Find it: search lockfiles, CI logs and package caches for agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2.
  • Assume every credential reachable from those machines and runners is exposed, not just Azure and GitHub; reports describe the stealer reading environment variables and local configuration more broadly2.
  • Rotate first, then investigate: review cloud audit logs and CI histories for use of those credentials since 17 November.
  • Rebuild affected environments rather than cleaning them, and pin to a verified version.

The CTO's take

This is the same lesson as the recent vendor access incidents, one layer down: trust granted for convenience becomes access for attackers. Package registries are run by the publishers you depend on, and their credentials can be stolen like anyone's. The defence is to assume a dependency will eventually be poisoned and design so that, when it happens, it finds nothing worth taking. item.title: Tech news, 19 November 2026: Java4Shell, a poisoned Microsoft agent package, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, and Malaysia's data centre pipeline
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Java4Shell exposes Java servers to remote code execution, Microsoft's agent-framework package is poisoned on PyPI, and OpenAI ships GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol.
item.content:encoded:
A flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder, dubbed Java4Shell, puts widely used Java servers at risk of remote code execution, and fixes are arriving unevenly across Java distributions. Two malicious releases of Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI stole cloud and CI credentials at Python start-up. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, and Malaysia's parliament heard how large its approved data centre pipeline has become.

Today's brief covers stories from 17 to 18 November.

1. Java4Shell puts Java servers at risk of remote code execution

Researchers at Calif disclosed CVE-2026-114938, dubbed Java4Shell, a flaw in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK's HotSpot runtime that can write outside its memory when handling malformed input; The Hacker News reports it can enable unauthenticated remote code execution in applications such as Jira, Jenkins and Keycloak1. Updated Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 builds were released on 17 November, and Qualys has published guidance on finding affected runtimes and patching2. Fixes are arriving at different times across Java distributions, and researchers note that turning it into working code execution takes work for each target1.

CTO take: the hard part is not the patch, it is finding every Java runtime: bundled inside vendor appliances, baked into container base images, pinned in old build pipelines. Start with internet-facing Java services and identity systems such as Keycloak, then rebuild images rather than patching running containers. Ask each vendor whose product ships its own Java when their fixed build lands, and track distributions separately, because Oracle's date is not your distribution's date. A software bill of materials that records the runtime, not just libraries, makes the next one of these a query instead of a hunt.

2. Microsoft's agent-framework package is poisoned on PyPI

Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of Microsoft's agent-framework package were published to PyPI on 17 November with a credential stealer that targeted Azure, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions secrets3. The code ran through a .pth start-up hook, so it executed whenever Python started on an affected machine, even if the package was never imported; Wiz says 1.26.0 is the latest safe version4. Both releases have been removed.

CTO take: treat any machine or CI runner that installed either version as compromised and rotate every secret it could reach, not only the ones the reports name. The structural fix is the same as for every recent package attack: pin versions with hashes, let new releases age before automatic upgrades pick them up, and give CI jobs short-lived, narrowly scoped cloud credentials rather than long-lived secrets in environment variables. Agent frameworks are now core dependencies with broad access, so they deserve the controls you apply to payment code. See AI model supply chain security and vendor admin access as perimeter.

3. OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol

OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra, aimed at demanding professional work, and GPT-6.2 Sol, aimed at everyday and routine multi-step tasks, available in ChatGPT and Codex for paid plans and through the API5. Coverage reports lower API pricing for Astra and tighter safeguards on higher-risk cybersecurity requests6.

CTO take: a two-tier release is an invitation to route, not to switch. Run both against your own evaluation set, send routine work to the cheaper tier and keep the larger model for tasks where it measurably wins. If your product relies on security-related prompts, test whether the new safeguards change behaviour before upgrading. See LLM model routing and evaluation sets that predict production.

4. Malaysia's parliament hears the scale of its data centre pipeline

Malaysia's Dewan Rakyat was told on 18 November that the country's Data Centre Task Force had approved 27 projects worth an estimated RM225.97 billion up to last month, with lawmakers pressing for those investments to bring high-skilled jobs and strengthen AI and cybersecurity capability7.

CTO take: for companies across Southeast Asia, more local capacity means more choice of region and potentially lower latency, but also more scrutiny of what those facilities deliver locally and who uses their chips. If you plan to host AI workloads in Malaysia, check power and water commitments, export control obligations and local skills expectations alongside price. See the Malaysia GPU cloud case study and my work in Singapore and Southeast Asia.

What I'd do this week

  • Inventory Java runtimes, including those inside vendor products and container images; patch internet-facing services first.
  • Search lockfiles and CI logs for agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2; rotate secrets wherever it appears.
  • Add hash pinning and a release cooling-off period to Python and JavaScript dependency updates.
  • Evaluate GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on your own tasks before changing defaults.
  • If Southeast Asian hosting is on your roadmap, add local policy and export control checks to provider selection.

I am a fractional CTO and AI architect based in India, the United States and the UAE, working globally. If any of these lands on your desk this week, analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: Your vendors' admin tools are your perimeter: what N-central, ScreenConnect, Qubole and Optimizely have in common
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Four incidents in a month came through tools vendors use to manage customers. A CTO's take on standing vendor access, how to inventory it and how to shrink it.
item.content:encoded:
In the space of a few weeks, attackers went after a remote management platform, a remote support tool, a data platform's cross-account roles and an experimentation tag. Different products, one pattern: each is a channel a vendor uses to act inside many customers at once. Most companies have more of these channels than they know, and none of them shows up on a firewall diagram.

Four incidents, one pattern

N-able took its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management environments offline on 9 November after proof-of-concept exploits for more than 30 alleged flaws were published, and told on-premises customers to take their servers down1. A week later, attackers were exploiting a new N-central chain within hours of its proof of concept appearing2.

Meanwhile Huntress reported a campaign against managed service providers' ScreenConnect servers: between 20 October and 16 November, attackers posing as guests made around 688,000 requests across 42 servers to push a malicious file, waiting for a technician to join a session so a flaw in the technician's client would run it3. Wiz reported that an attacker used credentials tied to Qubole's AWS account to assume roles customers had created to trust Qubole, then collected secrets and data4. And attackers used a flaw in Optimizely's sign-up flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects, which then ran on customers' websites5.

These are reported as four separate stories. They are one story. Each product is a channel a vendor uses to act inside many customers at once, and each attack went after the vendor's side of that channel rather than the customer's front door.

Where vendor access actually lives

Most organisations can list their suppliers. Far fewer can list what each supplier can do inside their environment right now, without asking. That second list is the one that matters.

The common property is that the access is standing: it exists whether or not the vendor is doing anything for you today, and it is protected by the vendor's security, not yours. A remote management agent that can run any command at any time is the same risk on a quiet Sunday as it is during a support call.

Put vendor actions through the same gates as your own

The useful model comes from platforms that already treat every caller the same way. In Kubernetes, every request to the API server, from a person or from a workload, passes authentication, then authorisation, then admission control before it changes anything7. Vendor access usually skips most of that: the agent is authenticated once at install and then trusted for everything.

Applied to suppliers, that means three questions for every channel. Who is acting: the vendor's platform, or a named technician with strong sign-in? What may they do: everything, or a defined set of actions on a defined set of systems? And what checks the action at the moment it happens: nothing, or a policy, an approval or at least a record someone reviews?

Cloud providers have built some of this already. AWS documents the confused deputy problem for exactly the Qubole pattern, and recommends conditions such as an external ID on roles that third parties assume6. That helps against one customer tricking a vendor into acting on another's account. It does not help when the vendor's own credentials are stolen, which is why narrowing what each role can reach matters as much as how it is assumed.

What to do: a short programme, not a project

ChannelThis month's exampleFirst thing to change
Remote managementN-central exploits1Limit which machines the agent covers and what scripts it may run
Remote supportScreenConnect technician attacks3Patch technician clients; block file transfer by guests; record sessions
Cross-account cloud rolesQubole roles assumed4Remove unused roles; keep secrets out of what roles can read
Third-party scriptsOptimizely injection5Keep vendor scripts off payment and login pages; restrict with a Content Security Policy

The test is simple: if a vendor told you at 3am that its platform was compromised, could you cut its access to you within the hour, and know what it had done in the last month? If not, start there.

The conversation with your managed service provider

Many mid-sized companies reach remote management and remote support tools only through a managed service provider, so the exposure is real but the controls belong to someone else. That makes the contract and the questions the control. Ask which tools they run on your systems and at what versions, how technician accounts sign in, whether sessions are recorded and whether you can see the logs, and how they would tell you about a compromise of their own tooling. The MSP cyber resilience case study shows what a provider that takes this seriously looks like from the inside.

For cloud and SaaS access, the same thinking runs through the third-party cloud access case study and the machine identity case study. For web scripts, see the payment page script security case study, and for AI vendors specifically, AI inference providers are now supply chain.

The CTO's take

Supplier risk is usually run as paperwork: questionnaires, certificates, annual reviews. This month showed it is an engineering problem. The question is not whether a vendor is reputable, but how much it can do inside your environment without you noticing, and how fast you can stop it. Those are things you can measure, reduce and rehearse.

item.title: Tech news, 18 November 2026: the Optimizely supply chain attack, Nvidia's first results without Huang, New York's AI enforcement unit and Microsoft's MAI Code 2
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: attackers inject malware via Optimizely into 178 sites, Nvidia beats and raises in its first post-Huang results, New York forms an AI enforcement unit.
item.content:encoded:
Attackers used a flaw in Optimizely's experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into the websites of 178 organisations, a reminder that every third-party script runs with your site's full trust. Nvidia reported strong results and raised guidance in its first quarter under an interim chief executive, New York set up a unit to enforce its AI safety law, and Microsoft released cheaper coding models.

Today's brief covers stories from 16 to 17 November.

1. Attackers inject malware into 178 websites through Optimizely

Optimizely said an unauthorised party exploited a flaw in its Experimentation account sign-up flow to inject malicious JavaScript into some customer projects; Report URI identified infected snippets across 178 organisations, including major media and technology brands1. The Register reports the code targeted visitors' payment details and cryptocurrency transfers, and Optimizely says it fixed the flaw, removed the code, revoked tokens and notified customers2.

CTO take: any third-party script on your site runs with your site's full trust. List every script you load, keep testing, analytics and marketing tags off payment and login pages, restrict what scripts can do with a Content Security Policy, monitor scripts for unexpected changes and make sure you can switch a vendor's tag off in minutes. Payment card rules already require monitoring of scripts on payment pages; this shows why. See the payment page script security case study.

2. Nvidia beats and raises in its first results without Huang

Nvidia reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion, with data centre revenue of $107.6 billion, and guided next-quarter revenue to about $130 billion3. CNBC notes it was the company's first report since Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, with Colette Kress serving as interim CEO4.

CTO take: demand for AI hardware is still rising, which means capacity stays tight and expensive for most buyers into next year. Plan for that: commit to capacity only where usage is proven, make models cheaper to run, and keep your stack portable across providers. See AI capacity contracts.

3. New York creates a unit to enforce its AI safety law

New York Attorney General Letitia James announced an AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement and Transparency unit, which her office describes as the first in the country dedicated to enforcing AI laws, and which will enforce the state's RAISE Act for frontier AI developers5.

CTO take: enforcement capacity is following the laws. The direct duties fall on large model developers, but expect providers to ask customers for help with incident reporting and to update terms. Keep a record of the AI models you use and how; see the board AI briefing checklist and the US page.

4. Microsoft releases MAI Code 2 for coding

Microsoft announced MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash at Ignite, available in GitHub Copilot, alongside other new MAI models; Microsoft's own benchmarks claim performance close to leading frontier models at a much lower price6.

CTO take: coding model choice is becoming a cost lever, not just a quality one. Test new models on your own repositories and tasks before switching, and keep your coding agent policy independent of any one model; see AI coding policy for engineering teams.

What I'd do this week

  • Inventory third-party scripts on your sites and remove any from payment and login pages.
  • Add or tighten a Content Security Policy and script change monitoring.

item.title: Tech news, 17 November 2026: US licences for AI chips to five countries, a Nordic AI gigafactory consortium, AMD closes World Labs and a nervous week for AI stocks
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: the US requires licences for AI chips to five countries, a Nordic AI gigafactory bid forms, AMD closes World Labs and AI stocks slide.
item.content:encoded:
The US moved to require licences for advanced AI chips going to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, including to curb remote access through overseas data centres. In Europe, five companies formed a consortium to bid for an EU AI gigafactory. AMD completed its purchase of World Labs, and AI stocks fell ahead of Nvidia's results and Anthropic's expected listing.

Today's brief covers stories from 15 to 16 November.

1. The US requires licences for advanced AI chips to five countries

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued a rule requiring licences for exports of advanced AI chips and the systems containing them to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, citing diversion risk, DCD reports1. Nextgov reports the rule also aims to stop controls being circumvented through remote access to data centres in third countries; reporting says companies headquartered in the US are exempt if they meet reporting requirements2.

CTO take: if you use or plan GPU capacity in South-East Asia or Brazil through non-US providers, expect new paperwork, delays and possibly higher prices. Ask providers how the rule affects their supply and existing contracts, and keep alternatives in other regions. If you operate data centres in these markets, know your customers and where their ownership sits. See AI capacity contracts and the Singapore page.

2. Five European firms form a consortium to bid for an EU AI gigafactory

Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda formed AI Gigafactory Northern to bid in the EU's AI gigafactory programme, proposing one AI facility spread across sites in the Nordic and Baltic region3. The Next Web reports initial sites in Finland, Estonia and Latvia, with a Swedish site to be confirmed4.

CTO take: European sovereign AI capacity is moving from policy to bids, but it will take years to arrive. If EU data residency or sovereignty matters to your customers, plan with today's providers and watch these projects as future options rather than near-term capacity. See the sovereign LLM platform case study and the Europe page.

3. AMD completes its acquisition of World Labs

AMD said it completed its acquisition of World Labs, which builds models that create and simulate interactive 3D environments, and that co-founder Fei-Fei Li joins AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist5.

CTO take: chipmakers are buying model and research teams to make their hardware more attractive. For buyers, more credible alternatives to a single accelerator vendor are good news, but only if your software stack can use them. Keep serving layers portable across hardware where you can.

4. AI stocks slide ahead of a big week

US tech stocks fell on 16 November, with AI-linked names hit hardest, ahead of Nvidia's quarterly results and Anthropic's expected market debut later in the week, CNN reports6.

CTO take: market swings rarely change engineering plans, but they shape the financing behind AI capacity and pricing. Keep contracts flexible and avoid building on a single provider whose economics you cannot see.

What I'd do this week

  • Ask GPU and AI cloud providers in South-East Asia and Brazil how the new US rule affects them.
  • Check where your AI capacity is planned and whether it relies on a single region or provider.
  • Review how portable your model serving is across hardware vendors.

item.title: Meta's €805 million fine: what on-device data, consent and AI features mean for product teams in Europe
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Italy fined Meta €805M for reading phone galleries without specific consent. A CTO's take on device access rules in the EU and how to design AI features around them.
item.content:encoded:
Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million because a Facebook feature, on by default, read photos, videos and metadata from Android phones without specific consent. The striking part is not the size of the fine but the principle: in the EU, reading data on a user's device needs consent even if nothing leaves the phone. As AI features look for more on-device context, that principle reaches far beyond Meta.

What the Garante decided

Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million over the Facebook Android app's gallery suggestions feature, which was on by default and proposed photos and videos from users' phones to post; the authority found it accessed photos, videos and metadata without specific, informed consent1. Meta must ask for consent through a separate, specific prompt, keep the feature off by default and report back to the regulator; Meta said it strongly disagrees and will appeal23.

The legal basis matters more than the number. The decision rests on the rule, from the EU ePrivacy Directive, that storing or accessing information on a user's device requires consent unless it is strictly necessary for a service the user asked for4. Reporting notes the authority treated that requirement as applying whether or not data left the phone1.

Why this matters beyond Meta

Many product teams assume that processing data locally is automatically privacy-friendly and needs no special permission. The European Data Protection Board's guidelines on the technical scope of the device access rule take a broader view: the rule turns on gaining access to information on the device, and the guidelines discuss local processing among their use cases5. On-device processing is often good privacy engineering; it is not, by itself, a consent exemption.

AI features make this sharper. Assistants that read photos to suggest posts, scan messages to draft replies, index files to answer questions or use sensors for context all reach into the device. The more context a feature uses, the more it looks like the gallery suggestions feature the Garante fined.

Designing AI features that use device data

Off by default. If a feature reads personal content from the device and is not strictly necessary for something the user explicitly asked for, ship it off and let users turn it on.

A specific, honest prompt. Ask at the moment the feature is first useful, in plain words: what will be read, why, whether anything leaves the device, and how to turn it off. The operating system's permission dialog is not enough on its own; it says what the app can access, not what your feature does with it. The same pattern works inside AI assistants: an in-context confirmation that says exactly what will happen before it does6.

Minimum access. Ask for the narrowest access that works: selected photos rather than the whole gallery, one folder rather than all files, approximate rather than precise location.

Records. Keep a record of what each user agreed to, when and in which version of the prompt, so you can show it later and re-ask when the feature changes.

Same rules for models. If device content is sent to a server or a third-party model, say so, minimise it and apply your normal data protection controls. If it is used to train models, that is a separate purpose needing its own basis.

On-device processing is good engineering, not a legal shortcut. In the EU, if your feature reaches into the phone, ask first, ask specifically and start switched off.

A quick review for existing features

CTO take

This fine is about consent and defaults, not about whether the feature was useful. As products add AI that looks for more context, the easiest way to stay on the right side of EU rules is to treat device content as something users lend you deliberately, not something you collect because the permission dialog allowed it. Product, engineering and legal should review device-reading features together, and new AI features should come with a consent design from day one. Meta has said it will appeal, so the decision may change; the design principles will not. Read alongside the 16 November tech news, the data protection programme case study and the Europe page.

item.title: Tech news, 16 November 2026: Italy fines Meta €805 million, Microsoft explains its outage, Maileva's 22 million-person leak and a new N-able exploit
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Italy fines Meta €805M over Android gallery access, Microsoft explains its outage, a La Poste unit leaks 22M records and N-able is hit again.
item.content:encoded:
Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million for accessing phone galleries without proper consent, a reminder that device permissions are personal data decisions. Microsoft gave a preliminary cause for last week's outage, a French mail platform confirmed a leak affecting 22 million people, and attackers exploited a new chain against N-able's remote management servers.

Today's brief covers stories from 13 to 15 November.

1. Italy fines Meta €805 million over Android gallery access

Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta €805 million because the Facebook Android app's gallery suggestions feature, on by default, accessed photos, videos and metadata on users' phones without specific, informed consent, Security Affairs reports1. Meta must ask for separate consent and keep the feature off by default; it said it strongly disagrees and will appeal2.

CTO take: in the EU, reading data from a user's device needs consent even if nothing leaves the phone. Any app feature that touches photos, contacts, files or sensors should be off by default, explained in a specific prompt and logged. As AI features look for more context from devices, this ruling sets the bar; product and legal should review them together. See the Europe page.

2. Microsoft gives a preliminary cause for its outage

Microsoft said traffic shifts during routine network maintenance exposed a latent bug from an earlier capacity upgrade, causing connection requests to queue until servers ran out of processing capacity; it found no sign of malicious activity3. ARN reports the disruption lasted about 30 hours and that Microsoft will publish a full post-incident review4.

CTO take: latent bugs exposed by later changes are among the hardest failures to prevent, even for the largest operators. The lesson for your own systems is to test changes against realistic load and to make rollback fast; the lesson for your suppliers is to plan as if this will happen again. See the Microsoft 365 outage playbook.

3. A La Poste subsidiary confirms a leak affecting 22 million people

Maileva, an online mail service in La Poste's Docaposte group, confirmed on 14 November that names and postal addresses of around 22 million people were stolen in a September attack, Ouest-France reports5. The people affected were recipients of mail sent by Maileva's business customers.

CTO take: if you send letters, invoices or notices through a print-and-post provider, your customers' data sits with that provider. Include such services in your supplier inventory, ask how long they keep recipient data and whether they need to keep it at all, and prepare to answer your own customers' questions.

4. A new N-able N-central exploit chain is in use

Attackers began exploiting a new chain against N-able N-central remote management servers, dubbed 4EverAble2Shell, within hours of a proof of concept being released, BleepingComputer reports6.

CTO take: this is the second wave against N-central in a week. If your managed service provider runs it, ask for confirmation that their servers are patched or offline, and consider restricting what their remote management agents can do on your systems until they are. See the third-party access case study.

What I'd do this week

  • Review app features that read device data and make sure consent is specific and defaults are off.
  • Read Microsoft's post-incident review when published and update your outage plan.
  • Add print, mail and notification providers to your supplier inventory.
  • Get written confirmation from your managed service provider about N-central.

item.title: Tech news, 15 November 2026: the Fireworks AI breach spreads to Cursor and Uber, phishing follows the Microsoft outage, Check Point's exploited zero-day and SpaceX's AI campuses
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: a leaked Fireworks AI key led to Cursor's breach and exposed Uber driver data, phishing used the Microsoft outage and a Check Point zero-day is exploited.
item.content:encoded:
The Fireworks AI breach is now showing up in its customers' disclosures: Cursor traced its own incident to a key it had given Fireworks, and Uber said driver records held by Fireworks were taken. Attackers used the Microsoft 365 outage as a phishing lure, a Check Point zero-day was exploited to gain root on gateways, and SpaceX announced plans for large AI computing campuses.

Today's brief covers stories from 12 to 14 November.

1. The Fireworks AI breach reaches Cursor and Uber

Cursor said its October breach began with an access key it had issued to Fireworks AI being exposed; the key gave read-only access to a shared storage bucket whose records still contained credentials, which the attacker used to reach some of Cursor's services and plant backdoored extensions1. Separately, Uber said driver records held by Fireworks AI, including driver's licence information, were taken, according to state breach filings2.

CTO take: this is what supply chain risk looks like in AI: one provider's breach becomes many customers' incidents. Never give an AI provider a key with more reach than it needs, never let logs or stored records keep live credentials, and know which of your data each provider holds so you can respond the day they disclose. See AI inference providers are supply chain.

2. Microsoft restores 365 services and warns of outage-themed phishing

Microsoft said Microsoft 365 services were restored for all remaining affected customers after the multi-day disruption, and warned of a phishing campaign exploiting it3. The emails imitated service-health notices, cited a real incident number and pressured recipients to follow fake email recovery links4.

CTO take: every big outage is followed by phishing that uses it. Tell staff that real status information comes from the admin centre or your IT team, never from an email link, and check your mail filters for the reported patterns. See the Microsoft 365 outage playbook.

3. A Check Point zero-day is exploited to take over gateways

CISA added CVE-2026-123039, a privilege escalation flaw in Check Point's Gaia OS, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 13 November6. BleepingComputer reports attackers combined it with other flaws to gain root on gateways through the Mobile Access portal and deploy a wiper aimed at VMware ESXi5.

CTO take: security gateways keep appearing as entry points this year, from Fortinet to Check Point. Apply the vendor's hotfix, disable portals you do not use, check gateways for signs of compromise, and make sure backups of virtualisation hosts are isolated from the networks a compromised gateway can reach. See the management plane hardening case study.

4. SpaceX plans more than $74 billion of AI computing campuses

SpaceX announced plans for AI supercomputing campuses in Arizona and Texas worth more than $74 billion, with the Texas site to generate its own electricity, The Next Web reports7. The plans still depend on local approvals7.

CTO take: new AI capacity is increasingly built with its own power to avoid grid limits and local opposition. For buyers, more capacity is coming, but late and unevenly; plan with several providers and regions. See planning around the AI capacity crunch and the US page.

What I'd do this week

  • Review keys and data you have given AI providers, and remove anything not needed.
  • Warn staff about outage-themed phishing and where real status updates come from.
  • Patch Check Point gateways and disable unused portals.
  • Check that virtualisation backups are isolated from gateway networks.

item.title: AI agents can now pay: what ChatGPT Wallet means for merchants, payment teams and anyone building agents
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: ChatGPT Wallet lets agents buy with approval and tokenised cards. A CTO's take on agent checkout traffic, fraud rules and approval design for merchants and builders.
item.content:encoded:
On 13 November, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, letting its agents complete purchases for users with approval each time and tokenised card credentials. Card networks have been building agent payment schemes for months. Agent-initiated checkout is no longer a demo: it is traffic that will reach your store, your fraud rules and your support team. Here is how to prepare, whether you sell online or build agents yourself.

What launched

ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI's agents complete purchases for users: people save a card, the agent shows the items, total and card before checkout, and the user approves each purchase; merchants and agents receive tokenised card credentials rather than the real card number1. It is rolling out first to eligible users in the US, and OpenAI plans to support purchases within preset spending limits later2. Cards from Visa, Mastercard and American Express work at launch3.

It lands on rails the card networks have been building: Visa and Mastercard launched agent payment programmes that issue tokens for approved agents and verify them at the network4. Reporting on the launch notes OpenAI warned that some sites may block agent purchases unintentionally and that fraud systems may flag legitimate agent orders2.

How an agent purchase flows

For merchants: four things to decide now

1. Welcome, tolerate or block agents. Bot protection tuned against scrapers will often block agent checkouts too. Decide your policy deliberately. If you want agent sales, learn to recognise verified agents, for example through signed agent requests, rather than opening the door to every bot.

2. Tune fraud rules for a new pattern. Agent orders can look unusual: fast, consistent, from new devices, with tokens rather than typed card details. Review rules that would decline them wholesale, and watch approval rates for agent traffic separately from human traffic.

3. Make product data agent-readable. Agents buy what your data says. Accurate structured data on price, stock, sizes, delivery and returns reduces wrong orders and disputes; see structured data for AI search.

4. Plan for after the sale. Returns, customer service and disputes stay with you. Make sure support can see that an order came through an agent and what the customer approved, so arguments about "I did not mean to buy that" can be resolved.

For anyone building agents that spend money

The approval step is the most important design decision. A good confirmation shows exactly what will happen, in plain terms, inside the conversation, and needs a deliberate action to proceed. MCP's Apps extension shows the pattern for any agent action: an interactive card in the chat that the user confirms5.

An agent that can pay is an agent that can be tricked into paying. Keep a human approval on every purchase until limits, allowlists and monitoring have earned the right to remove it.

Prompt injection matters more once money moves: a product page or email that instructs the agent to buy something is an attack. Treat every page the agent reads as untrusted; see prompt injection defence for agents.

Where this is heading

Expect three things: agent traffic growing first in the US and then elsewhere as networks and wallets expand; pressure to allow purchases within limits without per-transaction approval; and regulators asking who is liable when an agent buys the wrong thing. Payment and consumer protection rules differ widely by market, so merchants selling internationally should watch how each region treats agent-initiated payments. See where I work.

CTO take

For merchants, the cost of preparing is small: a deliberate bot policy, fraud rules reviewed for agent traffic, clean product data and support tooling that shows how an order was made. For agent builders, the hard part is not the payment API but the approval experience and the limits around it. Both groups should start now, while volumes are low enough to learn. Read alongside the 14 November tech news, idempotent payments and the agent-ready marketplace case study.

item.title: Tech news, 14 November 2026: Nvidia's CEO resigns, ChatGPT Wallet lets agents shop, Apify confirms a breach and the FBI recovers Binance funds
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, ChatGPT Wallet lets agents buy with approval, Apify confirms a breach and the FBI seizes $1.2B of Binance funds.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia's chief executive resigned, putting a leadership change at the centre of the AI hardware supply chain. OpenAI gave its agents a way to pay for things with approval each time, an automation platform confirmed customer data was accessed in an attack, and US authorities seized part of last month's record Binance theft.

Today's brief covers stories from 12 to 13 November.

1. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia's chief executive

Nvidia said Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately, and that CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement1. The resignation followed reports about Huang's conduct that Nvidia had been investigating; the board said it expects operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap to continue without interruption12.

CTO take: in the short term, chips already ordered will ship and roadmaps rarely change overnight. Over a year, a leadership change at the dominant AI hardware supplier can shift priorities, pricing and partnerships. This is a good moment to check how dependent your AI plans are on one vendor's hardware and software stack, and whether your serving layer could run on alternatives. See AI capacity contracts.

2. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet for agent purchases

OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its agents complete purchases for users: people save a card, review the items and total, and approve each purchase, while merchants and agents receive tokenised card credentials rather than the real card number3. TechCrunch reports it is rolling out to eligible US users first, and that OpenAI plans to support purchases within preset spending limits later4.

CTO take: agentic commerce is moving from demos to checkouts. If you run an online store, expect agent traffic at checkout: decide whether you will welcome or block it, make sure fraud rules do not reject legitimate agent purchases wholesale, and keep product data structured so agents describe it accurately. If you build agents, keep a human approval step for spending until you have strong limits and monitoring. See agentic infrastructure and the agent-ready marketplace case study.

3. Apify confirms customer data was accessed

Web automation platform Apify confirmed that customer data was accessed in a cyberattack, including salted password hashes, two-factor recovery codes, phone numbers and authentication tokens linked to Google and GitHub sign-ins, with limited card details, SecurityWeek reports5.

CTO take: recovery codes and sign-in tokens are as valuable as passwords. If your teams use Apify, rotate credentials and integration tokens, regenerate two-factor recovery codes and review connected GitHub and Google access. More broadly, list the automation and scraping tools that hold tokens to your code and accounts; they are part of your supply chain. See the third-party access case study.

4. US authorities seize $1.2 billion of the stolen Binance funds

The FBI said US authorities have seized more than $1.2 billion of the cryptocurrency stolen from Binance last month, which it attributes to North Korean hackers known as TraderTraitor, out of more than $2.7 billion frozen with help from crypto firms6. CyberScoop reports authorities also seized infrastructure used in a related social engineering operation7.

CTO take: recovery is welcome but partial; prevention still matters more. For anyone holding digital assets, the lessons from the Binance case remain custody design, withdrawal controls and resistance to social engineering of staff. See custody architecture lessons from the Binance hack.

What I'd do this week

  • Review how dependent your AI roadmap is on one hardware vendor's stack.
  • Decide how your checkout should treat AI agent purchases.
  • Rotate tokens and recovery codes for automation tools that have disclosed breaches.
  • List the third-party tools that hold tokens to your code repositories.

item.title: Microsoft 365 went down: what it broke, why it spread so far, and what to do before the next outage
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: What the November 2026 Microsoft 365 outage broke, why one supplier's failure spread so far, and a practical playbook for surviving the next productivity SaaS outage.
item.content:encoded:
On 12 November 2026, Microsoft 365 failed across regions for much of a working day: email, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot, and for some organisations the security tools that sit on top of them. Your core systems may have been healthy, yet work stopped because the tools people use to communicate, find information and sign in were down. This is what happened, why the impact was so wide, and a playbook for being ready next time, whatever suite you use.

What happened

Problems began with Exchange Online and spread to other Microsoft 365 services and regions on 12 November. Microsoft's advisories listed Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Defender XDR among affected services, and users also reported OneDrive problems13. Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, pushing load onto the rest, and that it had found no indication of malicious activity2. It paused deployments and worked on a configuration change to relieve an overwhelmed connection process3.

The disruption was felt worldwide, with users in Australia reporting problems into the next day4. Recovery was gradual and uneven, and Microsoft has promised a post-incident report with the root cause1. Business customers may be able to claim service credits, but generally need to ask5.

Why one outage reached so far

Most organisations no longer use a productivity suite only for email. Over a few years it has become the place where people talk, store documents, sign in, get AI help and often run security tooling. When it fails, the effects cascade.

The pattern is worth naming: the tools you use to manage an incident are often hosted by the supplier that is having the incident. Many teams discovered that their incident bridge, their contact list and their runbook all lived in Teams and SharePoint.

During an outage: the first hour

Avoid well-meant improvisation: staff forwarding company email to personal accounts, sharing files through unapproved tools or resetting passwords repeatedly. Outages are also a favourite moment for phishing that imitates the supplier's status messages, so warn staff to expect it.

Before the next one: the playbook

1. Map your dependencies. For each critical business process, list what it needs from the suite: email, chat, documents, identity, AI. Most organisations find identity is the biggest single point of failure, because it gates access to everything else.

2. Build an out-of-band channel and use it. Pick a messaging and paging tool from a different provider, with accounts for incident leaders, and use it for routine on-call so it works when needed.

3. Keep critical information outside the suite. Contact lists, escalation paths and top runbooks should exist somewhere that does not depend on it: a separate tool, an offline copy and a short printed card for on-call staff.

4. Plan emergency access. Keep a small number of monitored break-glass accounts that can reach critical systems if the main identity provider is unavailable, protected with hardware keys and tested regularly.

5. Detect independently. Do not rely on the supplier's status page or staff complaints. Simple synthetic checks against sign-in, mail and chat endpoints, run from outside your network, give you earlier warning and your own evidence6.

6. Give customers another route. A status page hosted elsewhere, SMS templates and a phone line mean customers hear from you even when email is down.

7. Decide what AI is allowed to be critical for. If teams rely on an AI assistant for routine work, decide what happens when it is unavailable, and make sure nothing that must happen depends on it alone.

8. Rehearse. Run a short exercise: "the suite is down for a day". It will expose gaps faster than any document review.

You cannot stop a supplier's outage. You can make sure it is an inconvenience rather than a crisis, by deciding in advance how you will talk, decide and serve customers without it.

Should you diversify away from one suite?

OptionBenefitCost
Stay on one suite, add fallbacksSimple, cheap, covers most riskFallbacks must be maintained and used
Separate identity providerSign-in survives a suite outageMore integration and licences
Second suite for critical teamsFull capability during outagesExpensive and confusing day to day

For most organisations, the first option, with careful attention to identity and emergency access, gives the best return. Regulated firms with strict recovery targets may need more; see the Singapore insurer case study and the AI provider resilience case study.

This week

  • Hold a 30-minute review: what stopped, what you improvised, what you would do differently.
  • Record the incident IDs and your impact, and decide whether to claim service credits.
  • Set up an out-of-band channel for incident leaders if you do not have one.
  • Export critical contact lists and runbooks to a location outside the suite.
  • When Microsoft's post-incident report is published, read it and update your plan.

CTO take

This outage was not a security incident, and it will be fixed. Its lasting value is as a free rehearsal: it showed every organisation exactly where it depends on one supplier, at no cost beyond a lost day. Use that evidence now, while people remember it, to fund the small fallbacks that turn the next outage into an inconvenience. item.title: Tech news, 13 November 2026: a long Microsoft 365 outage, EU rules for AI sandboxes, an exploited Xen Orchestra flaw and Nebius's spending plans
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: a long Microsoft 365 outage, EU rules for AI regulatory sandboxes, an exploited Xen Orchestra flaw and Nebius raising capex as AI cloud costs climb.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft 365 was disrupted for much of a working day, a reminder of how much of most companies runs on one supplier. The EU set common rules for AI regulatory sandboxes, a virtualisation management tool was exploited before many users had patched, and Nebius's results showed how much capital AI cloud capacity now demands.

Today's brief covers stories from 10 to 12 November.

1. Microsoft 365 suffers a long outage

Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services were disrupted for much of 12 November; Microsoft said servers failing automated health checks dropped out of service and pushed load onto remaining infrastructure across several regions, and reported no evidence of a cyberattack1. XDA reports Microsoft paused deployments while preparing a configuration change to relieve an overwhelmed connection process2.

CTO take: most companies now depend on one productivity suite for email, chat, files and increasingly AI assistants. You cannot prevent a supplier outage, but you can plan for it: an out-of-band way to reach staff and customers, critical contacts and runbooks available offline, and a clear decision on which processes stop and which continue. Review what broke for you on 12 November while it is fresh. See the supplier resilience case study.

2. The EU sets common rules for AI regulatory sandboxes

The European Commission adopted Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2487, published on 11 November, setting common rules for establishing and running national AI regulatory sandboxes under the AI Act3. EU Law Live reports the rules cover how sandboxes are set up, operated and supervised4; commentary notes participation produces documentation and an exit report rather than any compliance clearance.

CTO take: sandboxes are useful for testing novel AI systems with a regulator watching, especially for smaller companies, but they are not a shortcut to compliance. If you build high-risk AI for the EU, consider a sandbox for genuinely uncertain questions, and keep building your own evidence: risk assessments, evaluations and documentation. See the Europe page and the AI governance programme case study.

3. An exploited Xen Orchestra flaw exposes virtualisation hosts

Vates published advisory VSA-2026-062 on 10 November for an actively exploited authentication bypass in Xen Orchestra that lets attackers gain administrative access and take over XCP-ng hosts; SC Media reports exploitation leaves little trace in Xen Orchestra's own logs5.

CTO take: management consoles for virtualisation, backup and networking are the keys to everything beneath them, and many teams that moved to open-source hypervisors run them with less scrutiny than their old platforms. Patch to the fixed versions in the advisory, keep management interfaces off the internet and behind strong access controls, and check hosts for signs of compromise. See the management plane hardening case study.

4. Nebius raises spending plans as AI cloud capacity gets costlier

CTO take: specialist AI clouds are spending heavily ahead of revenue. For buyers, that can mean good prices today and more uncertainty later. Diversify across providers, prefer contracts that let you move, and watch the financial health of any provider you rely on for production capacity. See AI capacity contracts.

item.title: AI inference providers are now supply chain: what the NEAR AI and Fireworks breaches teach buyers
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Two AI inference providers disclosed breaches in a week. A CTO's take on what you hand a provider, what leaked and the questions to ask before trusting one with data.
item.content:encoded:
Within days of each other, NEAR AI and Fireworks AI disclosed breaches. One came through a flaw in an open-source inference engine running inside a confidential computing enclave; the other through a cloud provider hosting research machines, reaching customers' secrets, datasets and partial model weights. Most companies now send prompts, documents and fine-tuning data to providers like these. Here is what to learn, and what to ask.

What happened

Fireworks AI reported two October incidents. In the first, internal credentials were used to read environment variables in evaluation jobs for a limited number of customer accounts, which The Register reports included customers' API keys and tokens12. In the second, an attacker reached Fireworks' development machines through a cloud provider hosting its research machines, accessing billing records and, for a limited set of accounts, stored secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights13.

NEAR AI disclosed that an attacker used a remote code execution flaw in the open-source SGLang inference engine to run code on one inference server, where in-flight requests, including confidential-mode ones, could be observed; API keys for two customers were exposed through logs45.

What you hand an inference provider

Using an inference provider feels like calling an API. In practice, you often give them much more than prompts.

Four lessons

1. Do not give providers long-lived keys to other systems. Both incidents involved secrets stored with the provider: environment variables in evaluation jobs and stored secrets in accounts. If an inference job needs to reach another service, give it a short-lived, narrowly scoped credential, or call that service from your side instead. See the machine identity case study.

2. Send the minimum, keep the rest. Fine-tuning datasets uploaded months ago often stay with the provider long after the experiment ended. Delete what you no longer need, prefer providers that let you set retention, and remove personal data from training sets where you can.

3. Confidential computing is a layer, not a guarantee. The NEAR AI case shows that a flaw in the engine inside the enclave can still expose requests4. Ask providers how quickly they patch inference engines and what egress controls apply inside protected environments.

4. Your provider has providers. The second Fireworks intrusion came through a cloud provider hosting research machines1. Ask which third parties host the provider's infrastructure, including research and development environments, not just production.

Questions to ask before trusting a provider with data

AskWhy it matters
What do you store from my requests, and for how long?Logs and caches outlive the request
How are customers isolated from each other?One compromised account should not expose others
How fast do you patch inference engines?Engine flaws were the entry point at NEAR AI
How are secrets I give you stored and who can read them?Stored secrets were exposed at Fireworks
Which third parties host any of your environments?Development environments were the route in
How and when will you notify me of an incident?You need time to rotate keys and assess impact
Can I delete datasets and fine-tuned weights on demand?What is gone cannot leak

An inference provider is a data processor holding some of your most sensitive information. Choose and manage it the way you would a payments processor, not a developer tool.

If you use an affected provider

CTO take

AI providers have grown faster than their security, and attackers have noticed: LLMjacking gangs want keys, and fine-tuning datasets are valuable in their own right. The answer is not to stop using providers, but to treat them as critical suppliers: minimise what you send, avoid leaving secrets with them, demand clear answers on patching and third parties, and keep the ability to move. Read alongside the 12 November tech news, LLMjacking and stolen AI keys and the self-hosted inference security case study.
